chunks: "The photoelectric effect is when light hitting a material, classically a metal surface, knocks electrons out of it. What makes it famous is how it behaves.
If the light's frequency is below a certain threshold, no electrons come out, no matter how bright you make it.
Above the threshold, electrons come out immediately, and their maximum kinetic energy depends only on the frequency, not the intensity.
Brighter light just gives you more electrons. Einstein explained this in 1905 by treating light as photons, each with energy hf . One photon gives all its energy to one electron.
Part of that pays the work function , the energy to escape the surface, and the rest is kinetic energy: KE max equals hf minus . So if hf is less than , nothing escapes.
You can measure KE max as a stopping voltage, and plotting it against frequency gives a straight line with slope h over e .
For hardware, the version that matters is the internal photoelectric effect. In a semiconductor, a photon with energy above the band gap creates an electron-hole pair.
That's how photodiodes, solar cells and image sensors work, and it's why silicon can't see past about 1. 1 µm."
